extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, practitioners, and students interested in crowdsourcing design, use, and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, running, and assessing crowdsourcing projects across domains (market research, R&D, mapping, microtasks, competitions, etc.). Covers methods, platform types, motivations, demographic limits, quality-control and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection that engages contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that bug people, make people feel good about themselves, tap into niche knowledge of proud experts, and subjects that people find sympathetic tend to be successful crowdsourcing themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose problems that are emotionally or intellectually motivating to potential contributors. Examples include mapping earthquake zones, image identification, or niche expert challenges. Anti-pattern: dry or poorly framed problems that fail to attract interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs implicit crowdsourcing choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit crowdsourcing lets users work together to evaluate, share, and build specific tasks; implicit crowdsourcing means users solve a problem as a side effect of other activities (standalone or piggyback).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit approaches when you need conscious contributions, transparency, and collaboration (e.g., edit a wiki). Use implicit when low-effort, background data capture is acceptable (e.g., reCAPTCHA, data donation). Consider consent and ethics for implicit methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brabham problem-based typology (matching approach to problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four approaches: Knowledge discovery and management (assemble information), Distributed human intelligence tasking (HIT) (process/analyze existing info), Broadcast search (ideation with objective, provable right answer), Peer-vetted creative production (subjective ideation dependent on public support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the crowdsourcing method to task type: use broadcast search for solvable scientific problems, HIT for large-scale human annotation, peer-vetted production for design/aesthetic tasks. Each has distinct suitability and aggregation/selection needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform typology (Blohm's four platform types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing platforms can be categorized as Microtasking, Information Pooling, Broadcast Search, and Open Collaboration; they differ in diversity of contributions (homogenous vs heterogenous) and aggregation (selective vs integrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select platform type according to desired contribution diversity and aggregation method. Example: microtasking for repetitive annotation; open collaboration for collective resource building (e.g., OpenStreetMap).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step crowdsourcing process (Define, Broadcast, Attract, Select)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linus Dahlander, Lars Bo Jeppesen, and Henning Piezunka distinguish four steps in the crowdsourcing process: Define the problem, Broadcast it, Attract contributors, and Select outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design project planning around these steps. Invest time in clear problem definition and broadcasting to the right channels; plan selection criteria and methods in advance (e.g., expert review, voting, algorithmic ranking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdvoting method choice and bias awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple like-counting is easy but privileges early contributions; pairwise comparisons with ranking algorithms can avoid early-bird bias and are faster but are harder to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fairness to late contributors matters, prefer ranking algorithms or pairwise comparisons. Be mindful that complex algorithms may reduce transparency for participants. Example: Threadless used user voting to select T-shirt designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdfunding campaign presentation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns typically include a short video introducing the project, a list of rewards per donation, and illustrations/images to showcase the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear visuals and reward tiers to attract funders. Ensure messaging connects funders to the campaign's purpose (creative display, early access to products, community).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducement prize/competition design
rubrics_metrics.description: Web-based idea competitions often consist of a platform, generic problem statements, and cash prizes; best for ideation and solving problems with objective or provable answers (e.g., Netflix Prize, DARPA balloon challenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inducement prizes for well-defined problems with measurable success criteria and sufficient prize incentive. Plan for intellectual property and collaboration dynamics (collaborapetitive strategies may be needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit crowdsourcing forms (standalone and piggyback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standalone implicit crowdsourcing has users solve problems as a side effect of the task they're doing; piggyback takes data from third-party sites to gather information (data donation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implicit forms where unobtrusive data gathering is acceptable and ethical. Examples: ESP game for image metadata, reCAPTCHA for digitizing books. Ensure privacy and informed-consent considerations are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of university capstone programs vs open competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capstone programs are structured academic projects with faculty oversight, providing companies with student teams that deliver solutions as part of academic requirements; differ from independent competitors in supervision, scope, and participant motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer capstone programs when you need structured work, academic rigor, and potential talent scouting; expect the need for project scoping, faculty relationship-building, and integration of student output. Capstones may be lower-cost but require management to align with business objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative crowdsourcing suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative crowdsourcing sources people for creative projects (graphic design, architecture, product design, naming, writing); web platforms lower cost versus traditional methods but may raise quality concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use creative crowdsourcing for diverse idea generation and cost savings, but anticipate the need to curate, vet, and possibly compensate contributors fairly. Ensure clear briefs and selection criteria to get usable outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macrowork vs microwork task matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Macrowork tasks require specialized skills, fixed time, and are often part of visible projects; microwork tasks require minimal skill/time and pay small amounts (e.g., Mechanical Turk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match task complexity to the appropriate marketplace: microtasks for trivial, repetitive jobs; macrotasks for specialized, longer efforts (Upwork, capstone projects). Anticipate different quality expectations, costs, and participant motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile crowdsourcing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobile crowdsourcing uses smartphones and GPS for real-time data gathering, increasing reach but introducing urban bias and safety/privacy concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing mobile tasks, account for geographic bias (overrepresentation of urban users), privacy protections for location data, and participant safety. Employ task designs that minimize risk and respect local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project complexity categorization (simple vs complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple projects require more time/skill than micro/macro-work examples like writing a basic line of code; complex projects take most time, have higher stakes, call for specific skills (e.g., designing a patentable product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate higher pay and longer timelines to complex projects; recruit specialized participants; expect rarity of such offerings and corresponding higher management/integration costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdsourcing-based optimization challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization via crowdsourcing is challenged by worker heterogeneity: varied data quality and differing worker understanding complicate collaborative global optimization; methods like CrowdEC dispatch optimization tasks to worker groups for distributed evolutionary computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordination mechanisms and clear task formulations when attempting collaborative optimization. Anticipate aggregation difficulties and design for repeated interactions or specialist recruitment where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative/demographic limitations of the crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are often nonrandom and platform demographics vary (e.g., MTurk skewed by age, education, nationality); these skews affect generalizability and can bias results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess platform demographics before sampling; use stratified recruitment or multiple platforms to improve representativeness. Beware of participants masquerading as others to access tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations of contributors (intrinsic vs extrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic motivations include enjoyment-based (skill variety, task identity, autonomy, feedback) and community-based (identification, social contact); extrinsic motivations include immediate payoffs (money), delayed payoffs (future advantage), and social motivations (altruism, prestige).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incentive structures that align with likely motivations: small pay may be sufficient for some tasks, reputation or public acknowledgment may motivate volunteers, framing (e.g., 'help researchers identify tumor cells') can increase participation but may not improve quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation systems as motivators and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation and approval lists motivate higher-quality work by granting access to better tasks; conversely, rejection of bad work is necessary for the system to incentivize quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement reputation tracking and selective access to premium tasks, but ensure fair and transparent rejection policies. Note that many requesters fail to reject bad work, undermining the incentive structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to attract contributions risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Many initiatives attract few or no contributions; only the top percentile attracts frequent activity. Competition (e.g., Google Maps vs OpenStreetMap) can reduce participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan robust outreach and broadcasting; create clear value propositions and reduce friction. Monitor early activity and pivot strategy if contributions are low.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on product quality and need for curation
rubrics_metrics.description: Open participation allows unqualified participants, producing many unusable contributions; companies often must sort and manage low-quality submissions, increasing overhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include curation, vetting, and possibly use multiple workers per task or expert review as quality-control mechanisms. Balance openness with entry barriers to improve average contribution quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to malicious work and per-task incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay-per-task models can encourage speed over quality and enable targeted malicious behavior; verifying responses is time-consuming and often requires redundant assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks to detect low-effort or malicious submissions (attention checks, gold-standard items), consider vetting services (e.g., CloudResearch), and budget for redundancy or manual verification where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task design effects on accuracy (fixed classes vs free-form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling tasks with fixed classes restricts quality and can reduce accuracy; participants provide more accurate information at a more general level, and free-form responses often yield greater accuracy though may be less immediately usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of constrained and open-ended formats; include open-ended responses and attention checks to assess data quality. Choose classification granularity that balances usefulness for sponsors and accuracy from contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction between crowd and client
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of interaction between crowd and client often results in less information about the final product and reduced product quality; client interaction is considered vital in design processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where product quality matters, facilitate channels for feedback, clarifying briefs, and iterative engagement between crowd contributors and clients. Avoid purely transactional exchanges for complex design work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration tooling and knowledge-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of collaboration tools and workplace-like organization limits the crowd's ability to build upon each other's knowledge, reducing the quality of outputs compared to organized teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide collaboration platforms, versioning, and documentation to enable contributors to iterate and cohere work. For complex projects, structure teams or provide integrative roles to synthesize contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and labor concerns (low wages, worker rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical implications include low wages paid to crowdworkers, marginalization of crowd labor rights, and the risk of exploiting unpaid or underpaid contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider fair compensation, transparency on use of contributions, and respect for labor rights. Factor ethical costs into project budgeting and public-facing communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple evaluators/redundancy to improve data quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying responses often depends on having multiple workers complete the same task to correct errors; repeated vetting can control data quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan redundancy where single-pass work is unreliable; use majority-vote, gold-standard items, or expert adjudication. Be aware that redundancy increases time and monetary costs.
